title: Norbit
full_review:
In "Norbit" (DreamWorks), the mild-mannered titular nebbish (a bespectacled Eddie Murphy) has had an unusual upbringing in the Golden Wonton Restaurant Orphanage (a neon-illuminated roadside dive) by an eccentric-but-caring Mr. Wong (also Murphy).

When he grows up, he is browbeaten into marrying monstrously large battle-ax Rasputia (Murphy again) who, when they were children, had rescued him from schoolyard bullies.
Rasputia has three hulking brothers -- Big Jack (Terry Crews), Earl (Clifton Powell) and Blue (Lester "Rasta" Speight) -- who run a construction business and extort money from the town's terrified shopkeepers.

Rasputia, who turns out to be thoroughly evil (in fact, she's more scary than funny as vividly embodied by Murphy), blithely takes up with her dance instructor, inviting him to the house to commence an affair, and then going ballistic when the (till then) trusting husband Norbit dares accuse her of infidelity.

Eventually, Norbit reunites with his childhood sweetheart Kate (Thandie Newton), now grown up and beautiful, who comes back to town engaged to Deion (Cuba Gooding Jr.). Unbeknownst to Kate her fiance is an unscrupulous con artist whom the brothers draw into their scheme of acquiring the orphanage and turning it into a strip club.
You just know that by the film's end, battered husband Norbit will find it in himself to stand up to the villainously abusive Rasputia.

Director Brian Robbins -- working from a script by co-written by Murphy -- keeps the fitfully amusing gags coming, and Murphy's versatility is undeniably impressive, but the script often sags and vulgarity is rampant. (There are even two ex-pimp characters, Eddie Griffin and Katt Williams, stock characters who in the old days might have been gangsters, with irreverent names.)

The body suit with which Murphy is outfitted as Rasputia -- wince-inducing as it is, particularly when the couple accompany the orphans to a local amusement park, and she emerges in a bathing suit -- is all too realistic in its exaggerated contours and bulges. Still, it's a triumph for makeup guru Rick Baker.

How much compensation one finds in the heart beneath the visual and verbal bawdiness -- and elements of the film do have a sweetness that matches Norbit's appealingly gentle disposition -- will depend on a willingness to look beyond the flagged elements listed below that in less skillful hands would be even more offensive.

The film contains much low humor including some brief irreverence, crude language and expressions and some profanity, farcical adultery, brief rear male nudity, suggestive costuming, two "ex-pimp" characters, innuendo and some ethnic stereotyping. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.
